newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan economy in deep trouble despite optimism.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan economy in deep trouble despite optimism.

text.p: Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's arrival in power has fuelled optimism about reviving Pakistan's economy, but economists say dire problems cloud the horizon.
They fear the new government's declared determination to stimulate growth will put it on a collision course with the International Monetary Fund, which wants fiscal rectitude.
"Sharif seems to want to confront the IMF, which is the worst possible thing he could do," said a European ambassador.
Sharif, a 47-year-old industrialist, swept to office in February 3 elections in which his conservative Pakistan Muslim League routed Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party.
The business community has welcomed Sharif's victory, hoping he will restore political and economic stability after three years of drift and alleged corruption under Bhutto.
President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto on November 1, saying she had brought Pakistan close to economic collapse.
He installed a caretaker government, whose economic supremo Shahid Javed Burki said at the end of his three-month tenure that the economy had been "pulled out of a nose-dive".
The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index has risen 32.5 percent since January 1, largely on Sharif-linked expectations, though dealers say a technical correction is now overdue.

Sharif said on Wednesday his appeal to Pakistanis working abroad to remit at least $1,000 each through banks to help the shaky balance of payments had already brought in deposits worth $150 million, but there was no way to confirm the figure.

PML Secretary General Sartaj Aziz, expected to be the next finance minister, told the official news agency APP this week it was "not possible" to achieve the IMF-set target of cutting the budget deficit to four percent of Gross Domestic Product in fiscal 1996/97 from 6.3 percent in 1995/96.

Cutting the deficit would be a "by-product not an objective" of economic policy. "I will take all those measures to bring down the budget deficit which do not depress the economy and do not damage our competitive position," Aziz declared.
Such remarks have rung alarm bells at the World Bank and IMF, which resumed a stalled standby loan in December only after the caretakers pledged to meet the four percent deficit target.
Economists say the IMF, mindful of Pakistan's previous failures to meet agreed targets, is likely to give short shrift to any attempt by the new government to seek easier terms.
A rift with the IMF, which would be the second in less than two years, could have painful results, ranging from suspension of the standby loan to further cuts in Pakistan's credit rating.
Pakistan faces foreign debt repayments totalling about $1.5 billion in March to June, not including payments on military debt. Liquid foreign reserves now stand at $792 million.
Bankers say the current account deficit is likely to shoot beyond $5.0 billion in 1996/97 with foreign debt servicing reaching $2.25 billion and a trade gap of about $2.8 billion.
"Pakistan's external vulnerability has not been reduced in any way," said a regional economist, who asked not to be named.
"The trade account has not turned round, especially exports. Other inflows are down on last year, so the current account is not turning round, which means a haemorrhage of reserves."
To keep Pakistan afloat, the caretakers borrowed about $1 billion in December, often at shorter maturities and higher interest rates than the loans on which payments were due.

The new government hopes eventually to retire some of Pakistan's onerous foreign debt by privatising state assets, though Aziz has said this is a "long-term solution", requiring careful work to set up regulatory frameworks.
Despite heavy additional revenue measures imposed in October to secure resumption of the IMF standby loan, there are indications that revenue has already fallen behind target.
The Nation daily said this week the revenue shortfall could reach 35 billion rupees ($870 million) and take the deficit to at least 5.4 percent of GDP. The report has not been denied.
The regional economist said cuts might have to be made in hitherto sacrosanct areas such as military spending, which along with debt servicing, accounts for more than total net revenues.
"You absolutely have to tackle the fiscal problem up-front and you absolutely have to put in place mechanisms to reach the (IMF) targets," he said. "Fiscal policy is out of control."
